concepts.title: Hamming window
concepts.one_liner: The Hamming window is defined as $w[n] = 0.54 + 0.46 \cos(\pi n/L)$ for $n \in [-L, L]$, and zero otherwise.
concepts.content:
The **Hamming window** is defined as:
$$w  \left[n\right] =  \begin{cases}
    0.54+0.46 \cos (\pi n/L)     & \quad \text{if }  n \in  \left[-L, L\right] \\
    0       & \quad \text{otherwise }\\
\end{cases}$$
The Hamming window ($L=5$) produces a smooth transfer function with oscillations of smaller amplitude in the Fourier domain:
$$h = [1, 0.65, -2.45, -0.82, 8.8, 15, 8.8, -0.82, -2.45, 0.65, 1] / 29.36$$
concepts.motivation_md: The Hamming window reduces oscillations in the Fourier domain, producing a smooth transfer function useful in signal processing to minimize spectral leakage.
concepts.recap_md:
- The Hamming window is defined by $w[n] = 0.54 + 0.46 \cos(\pi n/L)$ for $n \in [-L,L]$.
- It is zero outside the interval $[-L,L]$.
- It produces a smooth transfer function with smaller amplitude oscillations in the Fourier domain.

concepts.title: binomial filter
concepts.one_liner: Binomial filters are good small anti-aliasing filters with a DFT profile like $1 + \cos(2\pi/N)$ and provide sufficient attenuation for most cases.
concepts.motivation_md: Binomial filters provide a practical, efficient way to reduce aliasing by attenuating high-frequency components, balancing smoothing and signal preservation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Binomial filter $b_2$ has a DFT profile $1 + \cos(2\pi/N)$.
- Gain at frequency $N/4$ is $1/2$, partially attenuating aliasing.
- Larger binomial filters like $b_4$ provide more attenuation but can oversmooth.

key_passage.text: In practice, when we need very small anti-aliasing filters, binomial filters are a good choice. The binomial filter $b_2$ has a DFT (length $N$) with a $1+\cos(2\pi/N)$ profile.

motivation.text: Therefore, the spectral content responsible for aliasing will not be completely removed, but the attenuation is enough in most cases.

example.text: Or $b_4 = [ 1, 4, 6, 4, 1]$, which attenuates the aliased frequencies even more, also results in an oversmoothed signal.

concepts.title: Downsampling
concepts.one_liner: Downsampling is applying an anti-aliasing filter followed by decimation.
concepts.motivation_md: Downsampling reduces data size while preventing aliasing by filtering before decimation, preserving signal quality.
concepts.recap_md:
- Downsampling = anti-aliasing filtering + decimation.
- Filtering is convolution with kernel $h_k$.
- Decimation selects samples at intervals $k$ in each dimension.

key_passage.text:
We will call **downsampling** the sequence of applying an anti-aliasing filtering followed by decimation: $$\begin{aligned} z[n,m] &= \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n,m\right] \circ h_k \left[ n,m \right] & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{conv}\\ \ell_{\texttt{out}}[n,m] &= z[kn,km] & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{decimation}
\end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: Nearest Neighbor Interpolation
concepts.one_liner: Nearest neighbor interpolation assigns to each output point the value of the closest input sample, resulting in a piecewise-constant image.
concepts.content:
In **nearest neighbor interpolation** we assign to
$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a,b)$ the closest value of the input
$\ell_{\texttt{in}}$:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a,b) = \ell_{\texttt{in}}[ n, m ]$$ where
$n-0.5<a<n+0.5$ and $m-0.5<b<m+0.5$. Note that here we are treating
$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a,b)$ as a continuous image. Nearest neighbor
interpolation results in an image that is piecewise-constant.
@fig-upsampling_and_downsampling-nn_interp shows the nearest neighbor
concepts.motivation_md: Nearest neighbor interpolation provides a simple, fast method to estimate values at non-integer coordinates by choosing the closest sample, useful for quick resizing or warping.
concepts.recap_md:
- Nearest neighbor assigns output value from the closest input sample.
- Output image is piecewise-constant.
- Coordinates satisfy $n-0.5 < a < n+0.5$ and $m-0.5 < b < m+0.5$.

concepts.title: Linear and Bilinear Interpolation
concepts.one_liner: Linear interpolation in 1D uses two nearest samples; bilinear interpolation in 2D uses four nearest samples via two linear interpolations.
concepts.content:
For 1D signals, the value of
$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a)$ is a result of linear interpolation between the
two closest input values $\ell_{\texttt{in}}[n]$ and
$\ell_{\texttt{in}}[n+1]$, where $n<a<n+1$. 


Interpolation is also a key operation when performing image warping.

For 2D signals, we have to
interpolate the output value $\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a,b)$ using four input
samples: $\ell_{\texttt{in}}[ n,m ]$, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}[ n+1,m ]$,
$\ell_{\texttt{in}}[ n,m+1 ]$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}[ n+1,m+1 ]$, where
$n<a<n+1$ and $m<b<m+1$.

**Bilinear interpolation** consists of first applying linear
interpolation to obtain $\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a,m)$ and
$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a,m+1)$ and then again applying linear
interpolation between those two values to obtain
$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(a,b)$. The result is illustrated in
@fig-bilinear_interp.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear and bilinear interpolation estimate values between samples to create smooth transitions, crucial for resizing and warping images.
concepts.recap_md:
- 1D linear interpolation uses two nearest input samples.
- 2D bilinear interpolation uses four nearest input samples.
- Bilinear interpolation applies linear interpolation twice, first on rows then on columns.

concepts.title: Expansion
concepts.one_liner: Expansion by factor $k$ inserts $k-1$ zeros between samples, increasing image size to $Nk \times Mk$.
concepts.content:
### Expansion

Expansion by a factor $k$ consists in increasing the number of samples in the image by inserting $k-1$ zeros between each sample on the horizontal dimension, and then on the vertical dimension. This will give us the image of size $Nk \times Mk$. We will use the notation:
$$\ell_{\uparrow k} \left[n,m\right]  = \ell\left[n,m\right] \uparrow k$$

Expansion is a linear operator that is the transposed to the decimation operation and is defined as:
$$\ell_{\uparrow k} \left[n,m\right] = 
 \begin{cases}
    \ell\left[n/k,m/k\right]     & \quad \text{if~} \text{mod} (n,k)=0 \text{~and~} \text{mod} (m,k)=0\\
    0       & \quad \text{otherwise }\\
  \end{cases}
$$
concepts.motivation_md: Expansion increases image resolution by inserting zeros between samples, preparing for interpolation to reconstruct a higher-resolution image.
concepts.recap_md:
- Expansion inserts $k-1$ zeros between samples horizontally and vertically.
- Resulting image size is $Nk \times Mk$.
- Defined by $\ell_{\uparrow k}[n,m] = \ell[n/k,m/k]$ if $n,m$ multiples of $k$, else 0.

concepts.title: Interpolation Filters
concepts.one_liner: Interpolation filters implement nearest neighbor and bilinear interpolation via convolution kernels applied to expanded images.
concepts.content:
### Interpolation Filters

When the upsampling factor $k$ is an integer value, interpolation using the methods described in section @sec-interpolation can be implemented using a convolution. The interpolation filters we will discuss here are separable, so the convolution kernel can be written as the product $h\left[n,m\right] = h\left[n\right] h\left[m\right]$:

As we discussed before, there are different interpolation methods: nearest neighbor, bilinear, and so on. In this section we will study them by looking at the convolution kernel needed to implement each interpolation method.

**Nearest neighbor interpolation** consists of assigning to each interpolated sample the value of the closest sample from the input signal. This can be done by convolving the expanded image from equation (@eq-upzeros) with the kernel (if $k$ is even):
$$h  \left[n\right] =  \begin{cases}
    1     & \quad \text{if }  n \in  \left[-k/2+1, k/2\right] \\
    0       & \quad \text{otherwise }\\
\end{cases}$$ This is very fast as it only requires replicating samples. But it gives very low quality. For $k=2$, the convolution kernel in 1D is $h  \left[n\right]=[1, 1]$

**Bilinear interpolation**: As we discussed before, bilinear interpolation is done in two stages: first, linearly interpolate each sample with the two nearest neighbors across rows, and then do the same for the columns. This can also be written as a convolution with the kernel (if $k$ is even): 

$$h  \left[n\right] =  \begin{cases}
    (k-n)/k     & \quad \text{if }  n \in \left[-k, k\right] \\
    0       & \quad \text{otherwise }\\
\end{cases}
$$ 

In the special case where $k=2$, the 1D bilinear interpolation kernel reduces to the binomial filter $h[n] = \left[1/2,1,1/2\right]$. And in 2D, for $k=2$, the kernel is $\left[1/2,1,1/2\right] \circ \left[1/2,1,1/2\right]^\mathsf{T}$. The binomial filter is not the best interpolation filter, but it is very efficient. When quality is important, there are better interpolation filters.
concepts.motivation_md: Interpolation filters allow efficient implementation of nearest neighbor and bilinear interpolation via convolution, enabling fast upsampling with varying quality.
concepts.recap_md:
- Interpolation filters implement methods via convolution kernels.
- Nearest neighbor kernel replicates samples, e.g., $[1,1]$ for $k=2$.
- Bilinear kernel for $k=2$ is the binomial filter $[1/2,1,1/2]$.

key_passage.text: When the upsampling factor $k$ is an integer value, interpolation using the methods described in section can be implemented using a convolution. The interpolation filters we will discuss here are separable, so the convolution kernel can be written as the product $h\left[n,m\right] = h\left[n\right] h\left[m\right]$

motivation.text: This is very fast as it only requires replicating samples. But it gives very low quality.

concepts.title: strided convolution
concepts.one_liner: Strided convolution involves convolution, decimation by taking every second pixel, and a ReLU nonlinearity.
concepts.motivation_md: Strided convolution combines filtering and downsampling efficiently, which is important in image processing and neural networks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Strided convolution applies convolution with a kernel.
- Then decimation reduces resolution by taking every second pixel.
- Finally, a ReLU nonlinearity is applied.

key_passage.text: This system has three steps: the first step is a vertical edge filter (convolution of the input, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$, with a horizontal kernel, $[1, -1]$). The next step is to reduce the resolution of the filter output by taking one pixel every two along each dimension (this operation is called decimation).

motivation.text: Decimation takes an input, $u$, with size $N\times M$, and outputs, $h$, with half the size $N/2 \times M/2$.

concepts.title: Decimation
concepts.one_liner: Image decimation changes image resolution by dropping samples, reducing size by a factor $k$.
concepts.content:
Image decimation consists of changing the resolution of an image by dropping samples. Decimation of an image of size $N \times M$ by a factor of $k$, where $N$ and $M$ are divisible by $k$, results in a lower resolution image of size $N/k \times M/k$:
$$\ell_{\downarrow k} \left[n,m\right]  = \ell\left[kn, km\right]$$
It is common to use the notations
$\ell_{\downarrow k} \left[n,m\right]   = \ell\left[n,m\right] \downarrow k = \ell\left[kn,km\right]$
to denote the decimation operator by a factor $k$. Decimation could be
concepts.motivation_md: Decimation reduces image resolution by dropping samples, a fundamental operation in image downsampling and processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- Decimation reduces image size by dropping samples.
- For factor $k$, size changes from $N \times M$ to $N/k \times M/k$.
- Notations include $\ell_{\downarrow k}$ and $\ell \downarrow k$.

concepts.title: delta train
concepts.one_liner: The delta train is a discrete pattern marking samples retained after decimation.
concepts.content:
$\ell_{\delta_k} \left[n,m\right]$, of same size as the input image, $N \times M$, where we set to zero the samples that will be removed in the decimation operation: 
$$\begin{aligned}
\ell_{\delta_k} \left[n,m\right] &= \ell\left[n,m\right] \sum_{s=0}^{N/k-1} \sum_{r=0}^{M/k-1} \delta \left[n - sk \, ,m - rk \right] \\
&=  \ell\left[n,m\right]  \delta_k \left[n,m\right]\end{aligned}$$ where $\delta_k \left[n,m\right]$ is the discrete version of the **delta train**.
concepts.motivation_md: The delta train identifies which samples remain after decimation, enabling precise representation of downsampled images.

- The delta train is a discrete pattern marking retained samples.
- It zeros out samples removed by decimation.
- Defined as $\delta_k[n,m] = \sum_{s,r} \delta[n-sk,m-rk]$.

concepts.title: Anti-Aliasing Filters
concepts.one_liner: Anti-aliasing filters blur images before downsampling to remove high-frequency content that causes aliasing.
concepts.content:
### Anti-Aliasing Filters

Anti-aliasing filtering is an essential operation whenever we manipulate the resolution of an image. When decimating a signal of size $N \times N$ with a scaling factor $k$, aliasing is produced by all the content at frequencies that are above $u,v > N/2k$. Therefore, to reduce aliasing, we have to remove any spectral content of the signal present at high spatial frequencies. We will do so by using an anti-aliasing filter that will blur the image before downsampling. Blurring removes high-spatial frequencies in the image.

The ideal anti-aliasing filter is a box in the Fourier domain with a cut-off frequency of $L=N/(2k)$ (using the notation introduced in @sec-sampling). The inverse Fourier transform of a box in the frequency domain, with width $2L+1=N/k+1$, is the **discrete sinc** function of length $N$ in the spatial domain:
$$\frac{1}{N} \frac 
{\sin(\pi n (N/k+1)/N)}
{\sin(\pi n/N)}
\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} 
box_{N/2k} \left[ u \right]$$

In 2D, the ideal anti-aliasing filter is separable and is obtained by two consecutive 1D convolutions along each dimension. The discrete sinc is very similar to the continuous sinc described in @sec-sampling. The discrete sinc is periodic, with period $N$. The following plot (@fig-discretesinc) shows the anti-aliasing sinc for $N=32$ and $k=2$ and the magnitude of its Fourier transform:

(see figure: Discrete sinc function for $N=32$ and $k=2$ and the magnitude of its DFT.)

And for $k=4$, the impulse response becomes wider and its Fourier transform has a lower cut-off frequency, $N/2k = 4$:

(see figure: Discrete sinc function for $N=32$ and $k=4$ and the magnitude of its DFT.)

One disadvantage of the ideal anti-aliasing filter is that the it requires convolving the image with a very large filter (as large as the image). We would like to use smaller filters to reduce the computational cost. One method to design anti-aliasing filters with a finite impulse response is to use a window, $w [n]$, and to use as anti-aliasing filter the kernel $w [n] h[n]$, where $h[n]$ is the impulse response of the ideal anti-aliasing filter. Typical windows used are the rectangular, Hamming, Parzen, or Kaiser windows.

The rectangular window sets to zero all the values outside of the interval $\left[-L, L\right]$. When $L=5$, it gives a tap-11 filter (a filter with an impulse response of length 11) with the following profile:

![Kernel $w [n] h[n]$, where $h[n]$ is a sinc and $w [n]$ is a rectangular window of length 11.](figures/upsamplig_downsampling/kernel_sinc_window.png){#fig-discretesinc width=100%}

The Fourier transform of the windowed impulse response, $w [n] h[n]$, is the convolution of Fourier transforms. The Fourier transform of the rectangular window is a sinc function. Therefore, the resulting Fourier transform is the convolution of the rectangle with the sinc function, which produces a smooth rectangle with some oscillations. Using other windows allows trading off the smoothing of the ideal rectangular form of the ideal low-pass filter and the oscillations.

The **Hamming window** is defined as:
$$w  \left[n\right] =  \begin{cases}
    0.54+0.46 \cos (\pi n/L)     & \quad \text{if }  n \in  \left[-L, L\right] \\
    0       & \quad \text{otherwise }\\
\end{cases}$$ The Hamming window ($L=5$) produces a smooth transfer function with oscillations of smaller amplitude in the Fourier domain:
$$h = [1, 0.65, -2.45, -0.82, 8.8, 15, 8.8, -0.82, -2.45, 0.65, 1] / 29.36$$

(see figure: Hamming window ($L=5$) and the magnitude of its DFT.)

In practice, when we need very small anti-aliasing filters, binomial filters are a good choice. The binomial filter $b_2$ has a DFT (length $N$) with a $1+\cos(2\pi/N)$ profile. At the frequency $N/4$ the gain is $1/2$. Therefore, the spectral content responsible for aliasing will not be completely removed, but the attenuation is enough in most cases.


![The binomial kernel $b_2 = \left[1,2,1\right]$, and its DFT.](figures/upsamplig_downsampling/binomial_kernel1.png){#fig-discretesinc2 width=100%}

Or $b_4 = [ 1, 4, 6, 4, 1]$, which attenuates the aliased frequencies even more, also results in an oversmoothed signal.

![The binomial kernel $b_4 = [ 1, 4, 6, 4, 1]$, and its DFT.](figures/upsamplig_downsampling/binomial_kernel4.png){#fig-discretesinc4 width=100%}

When implementing 2D anti-aliasing filters, we apply two consecutive 1D convolutions along each dimension. For efficiency, the anti-aliasing filter only needs to be computed on the samples that will be kept after downsampling ($k$-strided convolution). The necessary amount of attenuation of the aliasing frequencies will have to be decided based on each application.


In 2D, we can apply the binomial filter $b_2$ on each dimension,
$\left[1,2,1\right]/4 \circ \left[1,2,1\right]^\mathsf{T}/4$.


(see figure: Output of three different low-pass anti-aliasing filters. (left) Ideal low-pass filter. (center) Hamming window. (right) Binomial filter.)

The images in @fig-ringing_artifacts show the output of three different low-pass anti-aliasing filters. Note how the ideal low-pass filter introduces **ringing artifacts** in the output image (@fig-ringing_artifacts[a]). Despite that it removes frequencies that will produce aliasing after downsampling, it does that at a high cost because it introduces undesired image structures, which is exactly what we want to prevent with the anti-aliasing filter. The Hamming windowed sinc (shown in @fig-ringing_artifacts[b]) reduces the oscillation but there is still a halo present around edges. This is because there is still one oscillation on the filter impulse response. @fig-ringing_artifacts (c) shows the result applying am anti-aliasing binomial filter.

For most applications using a binomial filter ($b_2$ or $b_4$) is enough because it reduces aliasing and it does not introduce undesired image structures.
concepts.motivation_md: Anti-aliasing filters prevent aliasing artifacts by removing high-frequency content before downsampling, ensuring image quality.
concepts.recap_md:
- Anti-aliasing filters blur images to remove high frequencies causing aliasing.
- The ideal filter is a discrete sinc with a box-shaped frequency response.
- Practical filters use windowing or binomial filters to reduce computation and artifacts.

concepts.one_liner: The discrete sinc function is the inverse Fourier transform of a box filter and is used as an ideal anti-aliasing filter.
concepts.motivation_md: The discrete sinc function models the ideal anti-aliasing filter in the spatial domain, enabling perfect frequency cutoff before downsampling.
concepts.recap_md:
- The discrete sinc is the inverse Fourier transform of a box filter.
- It is periodic with period $N$.
- The ideal 2D anti-aliasing filter is separable into 1D convolutions.

concepts.motivation_md: Lanczos interpolation is a method used to improve image resampling quality by reducing artifacts during interpolation.
concepts.recap_md: - Lanczos interpolation is a specific interpolation technique.

concepts.title: Upsampling
concepts.one_liner: Upsampling consists in the sequence of expansion followed by interpolation.
concepts.motivation_md: Upsampling is used to increase the resolution of a signal or image by expanding it and then interpolating to fill in new values, enabling finer detail representation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Upsampling involves expansion followed by interpolation.
- Expansion is denoted as $z[n,m] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n,m] \uparrow k$.
- Interpolation is performed by convolution: $\ell_{\texttt{out}}[n,m] = z[n,m] \circ h_k[n,m]$.
